128581.q: What is the highest deductible that adults can choose in basic insurance?
128581.e: The highest deductible adults can choose is 2500 francs. The lowest is 300 francs.

128582.q: Sara has a deductible of 300 francs. Her first doctor's bill of the year is 120 francs. Who pays?
128582.e: The bill is smaller than the deductible of 300 francs. So Sara pays all of it herself.
128582.m: Below the deductible, you pay yourself.

128583.q: When can you normally change the deductible in basic insurance?
a: At the start of a new year
128583.e: You can change the deductible from 1 January. If you want a lower deductible, you must tell the insurer by the end of November.
128583.m: Change your deductible: at New Year.

128584.q: What percentage of the costs do you normally pay as a co-payment in basic insurance?
128584.e: The normal co-payment is 10 % of the costs above the deductible. There is an upper limit per year.

128585.q: Tim is 12 and has a deductible of 0 francs. His doctor's bill is 200 francs. How much do his parents pay?
128585.e: With a deductible of 0 francs, only the 10 % co-payment applies. 10 % of 200 francs is 20 francs.

128586.q: Anna has a deductible of 300 francs. Her costs for the year are 1300 francs. How much does she pay herself?
128586.e: First she pays the 300 franc deductible. Of the remaining 1000 francs she pays a 10 % co-payment, which is 100 francs. Together that makes 400 francs.

128587.q: What is true of the co-payment for children?
a: Its yearly limit is lower than for adults
Children pay half of every bill
For children it has no upper limit
128587.e: Children also pay a 10 % co-payment. But each year it is limited to half the amount for adults, which is 350 francs.
128587.m: For children, the co-payment has a lower limit.

128588.q: What makes up cost sharing in basic insurance?
128588.e: Cost sharing is what you pay yourself towards your own treatment: the deductible and the co-payment. The premium does not count.

128589.q: Why do you have to share the costs even though you pay premiums?
a: So that people do not go to the doctor unnecessarily
Because otherwise the health insurer closes
Because otherwise you do not get a card
128589.e: People who pay part themselves think more carefully about whether a doctor's visit is needed. That helps keep health costs, and so premiums, lower.
128589.m: Paying a share makes people careful.

128590.q: What may a health insurer do with supplementary insurance that is forbidden with basic insurance?
128590.e: With supplementary insurance, the insurer may ask health questions and turn people down. In basic insurance it must accept everyone.
128590.m: Supplementary: the insurer may say no.

128591.q: What do parents often take out supplementary insurance for, for their child?
a: For the normal check-up at the family doctor
128591.e: Basic insurance usually does not pay for braces. That is why many parents take out dental supplementary insurance early.
128591.m: Braces? That is usually a matter for supplementary insurance.

128592.q: Does supplementary insurance have to be with the same health insurer as basic insurance?
a: No, it can be with a different insurer
Only children may have different insurers
Yes, otherwise the basic insurance lapses
128592.e: Basic insurance and supplementary insurance are separate. You can have them with different health insurers.
128592.m: Basic and supplementary can live apart.

128593.q: You would like a hospital room with fewer beds (semi-private). Which insurance do you need for that?
128593.e: Basic insurance pays for the general ward in hospital. For semi-private or private you need supplementary insurance.
128593.m: More comfort in hospital: supplementary insurance needed.

128594.q: Can you cancel supplementary insurance without losing basic insurance?
a: No, then you are no longer insured at all
128594.e: Supplementary insurance is a separate contract. If you cancel it, the basic insurance stays in place.

128595.q: Mia wants to take out her supplementary insurance with a new insurer. What should she do first?
a: Wait for the new acceptance, then cancel
128595.e: Because the new insurer may turn people down for supplementary insurance, you should get accepted first. Only after that do you cancel the old supplementary insurance.
128595.m: Switching supplementary: first acceptance, then cancellation.

128596.q: What is written on the insurance card, among other things?
a: Your name and your insurance number
128596.e: The card shows your name, date of birth, insurance number and health insurer. So the doctor or pharmacy can bill the costs.
128596.m: The card says who I am and where I am insured.

128597.q: Where do you typically show your insurance card?
a: At the pharmacy when collecting medicines
128597.e: With the card, the pharmacy bills the health insurer directly. You also need it at the doctor's surgery and in hospital.
128597.m: Pharmacy, doctor, hospital: show your card.

128598.q: What can you often find on the back of the Swiss insurance card?
128598.e: The back is usually the European Health Insurance Card. It helps with treatment in EU and EFTA countries.
128598.m: The back: a holiday helper for Europe.

128599.q: What should you do if you have lost your insurance card?
a: Tell the health insurer and order a new one
128599.e: If you lose it, you contact the health insurer. It sends a new card. You must never use someone else's card.

128600.q: In Switzerland, do you get help in an emergency even without an insurance card?
a: Yes, in an emergency you are always treated
No, no card means no help
Only with cash in your pocket
Only if your parents are with you
128600.e: In an emergency you are treated even if you do not have your card with you. The details can be provided later.
128600.m: An emergency comes before the card.

128601.q: Why is the premium usually lower in the family doctor model?
a: Because you partly give up the free choice of doctor
Because family doctors work for free
Because only children may choose this model
128601.e: The family doctor coordinates the treatment, which often saves costs. In return, you give up going straight to any specialist.

128602.q: Elias has the family doctor model and has bad stomach pains in the night. May he go straight to A&E?
a: No, never without the family doctor
Only with a letter from school
128602.e: In a real emergency you may always go straight to A&E. The rules of the model apply to normal treatment.

128603.q: What is the same in all models of basic insurance?
a: The phone number of the advice line
128603.e: Whether standard, family doctor or Telmed: basic insurance always pays the same benefits. Only the route to treatment and the premium change.

128604.q: What is the model called in which you can go straight to any doctor without restrictions?
a: Standard model with free choice of doctor
128604.e: In the standard model you have free choice of doctor. In return the premium is usually higher than in the other models.

128605.q: What can happen if, in the family doctor model, you go straight to a specialist without a reason?
a: The insurer may not pay for the treatment
The premium is halved at once
128605.e: If you do not follow the rules of the model, you risk the insurer not paying or having to switch to the standard model.
128605.m: It pays to follow the model's rules.

128606.q: Lea is 13 and breaks her arm while cycling. Which insurance pays?
a: The health insurance with accident cover
128606.e: Children are not insured against accidents through an employer. That is why health insurance also pays for their accidents.

128607.q: Jonas works 4 hours a week. He hurts himself playing football at the weekend. Who pays?
128607.e: Under 8 hours a week, you are only insured through your employer for accidents at work. Accidents in your free time are then paid by health insurance.
128607.m: Few hours: free-time accidents through health insurance.

128608.q: An apprentice works 40 hours a week at her training company. She falls while skiing on holiday. Who pays?
a: The accident insurance through the training company
Her parents entirely on their own
128608.e: Apprentices are employees. If they work at least 8 hours a week, they are also insured against accidents in their free time through the training company.
128608.m: Apprenticeship means: accidents through the company.

128609.q: Why can you sometimes exclude accident cover from your health insurance?
a: Because you are already insured against accidents through your employer
Because accidents are banned in Switzerland
Because the municipality pays for everything
128609.e: Anyone insured against accidents through their employer does not need accident cover from the health insurer. Excluding it lowers the premium.

128610.q: What counts as an accident for health insurers?
a: A sudden, unintended injury from outside
128610.e: An accident is a sudden event from outside that injures the body, for example a fall. An illness, on the other hand, develops inside the body.
128610.m: An accident comes suddenly from outside.

128611.q: Why does brushing your teeth well also pay off financially?
a: Because basic insurance usually does not pay for dental treatment
Because the toothbrush gives money back
Because then the premium is zero
128611.e: You usually pay for holes and fillings yourself. People who look after their teeth well need fewer expensive treatments.

128612.q: What do many municipalities or schools offer children?
128612.e: Many municipalities organise regular dental check-ups for schoolchildren. That way problems are spotted early.
128612.m: School dentist: check early, save later.

128613.q: Ali falls off his scooter and breaks a tooth. What usually applies?
a: As an accident, the accident cover pays for the tooth
Nobody ever pays for tooth accidents
The school has to pay for everything
128613.e: Damage to teeth caused by an accident is paid by accident insurance. For children, that is the accident cover of the health insurance.
128613.m: Tooth damaged in an accident: accident insurance.

128614.q: What applies in basic insurance to glasses for children?
a: The insurer pays a contribution towards them
The insurer pays for every pair of glasses in full
Children are not allowed to wear glasses
128614.e: For children and young people up to 18, basic insurance pays a contribution towards glasses or contact lenses if a doctor prescribes them.

128615.q: Does basic insurance pay for new lenses for healthy adults?
a: Yes, a new pair of glasses every year
128615.e: For adults, basic insurance only pays for glasses in the case of certain illnesses. Otherwise you need supplementary insurance or pay yourself.
128615.m: Glasses for adults: often a matter for supplementary insurance.

128616.q: What does a child usually need so that the insurer pays towards glasses?
128616.e: The health insurer pays its contribution if the glasses were prescribed by a doctor. That is why you have your eyes tested first.

128617.q: What should you do when a doctor's bill arrives at home?
a: Check the bill and keep it
Throw it away unread at once
128617.e: You check whether the treatment is correct and keep the bill. Depending on the system, you pay it and then send it to the insurer.
128617.m: Read, check and keep the bill.

128618.q: What does a refund from the health insurer mean?
a: The insurer pays you back money for a bill you have paid
You give the insurer money as a present
You get your premium back every year
128618.e: If you have paid a bill yourself, you send it to the insurer. It pays you back its share, minus the deductible and co-payment.

128619.q: How can you submit a doctor's bill to many health insurers today?
a: Only in person at head office
Only by fax on a Sunday
Not at all, it is forbidden
128619.e: Many health insurers offer an app that lets you photograph and send the bill. Post works too.
128619.m: Submitting a bill: app or postbox.

128620.q: What does it mean when the pharmacy bills the health insurer directly?
a: The insurer pays the pharmacy, and you pay your share later
You never have to pay anything
The pharmacy gives you the medicines for free
The bill goes to your school
128620.e: The insurer pays the pharmacy directly. Afterwards it sends you a statement for your share, meaning the deductible and co-payment.
128620.m: Billed directly does not mean free.

128621.q: What can you do if a doctor's bill lists a treatment you did not have?
a: Ask the surgery or the insurer
128621.e: Bills can contain mistakes. You ask the doctor's surgery or the health insurer. That also helps save costs.

128622.q: What is a benefits statement from the health insurer?
a: An overview of what the insurer paid and what you pay
128622.e: The benefits statement shows the bill amounts, the insurer's share and your own share of the deductible and co-payment.

128623.q: Why is it worth sending doctor's bills to the insurer even when they are below the deductible?
a: So the insurer counts them towards the deductible
Because otherwise the insurer forbids them
So the premium falls at once
128623.e: The insurer adds the bills together. That way it knows when the deductible has been reached and it starts to pay.
128623.m: Submit all bills, even small ones.

128624.q: Who is responsible for premium reductions?
a: The canton you live in, together with the Confederation
128624.e: The cantons pay out premium reductions, and the Confederation contributes money. The rules differ from canton to canton.
128624.m: Premium reductions: a matter for the canton.

128625.q: The Rossi family has little money and three children. What could help them with health insurance premiums?
a: Applying to the canton for a premium reduction
128625.e: Families on a low income can get a premium reduction. In some cantons you have to apply for it, in others it comes automatically.
128625.m: Do not cancel, get help instead.

128626.q: Which statement about premium reductions is true?
a: The rules differ from canton to canton
They are the same amount in every canton
You only get them after an accident
128626.e: Each canton decides for itself who gets how much of a premium reduction. That is why it is worth asking your own canton.

128628.q: Why do many people switch health insurer for their basic insurance?
a: To get a new house number
128628.e: The benefits of basic insurance are the same everywhere. But switching can often save on the premium.

128629.q: What is the safest way to send your cancellation to the health insurer?
a: By text message to a friend
By word of mouth at the bus stop
Not at all, the insurer notices by itself
128629.e: With a registered letter you can prove that the cancellation arrived in time.

128630.q: What is sensible before cancelling your basic insurance?
128630.e: Switching is only worthwhile if the new insurer is cheaper. So you first compare the premiums for where you live.

128631.q: If you switch basic insurance, what happens to the supplementary insurance at the old insurer?
a: It stays in place unless you cancel it
128631.e: Basic and supplementary insurance are separate contracts. The supplementary insurance stays as long as you do not cancel it yourself.

128632.q: After switching basic insurance, what must you show when you have treatment?
a: The card of the new insurer
The card of the old insurer
128632.e: From the switch onwards, the new insurer is responsible. So you show the new insurance card at the doctor's and the pharmacy.

128633.q: What does solidarity mean in health insurance?
a: Healthy people help pay for the care of the sick with their premiums
Everyone pays only their own costs
128633.e: Everyone pays premiums into a shared pot. From it, the costs of people who are ill at the moment are paid.
128633.m: Everyone pays in, and whoever is ill gets help.

128634.q: Why does health insurance only work if many people take part?
a: Because the costs are spread across many people
Because doctors only treat large groups
Because otherwise the insurer does not print cards
Because you never get ill on your own
128634.e: The more people pay premiums, the better the high costs of individual sick people can be covered. That is the idea of insurance.
128634.m: Many together carry what one alone cannot.

128635.q: Which example shows solidarity in basic insurance?
a: Young, healthy people pay the same as people who are often ill
Healthy people get everything back at the end
Every person has their own insurer
128635.e: In basic insurance you pay regardless of your health. So healthy people help carry the costs of the sick.
128635.m: Same premium for all, however healthy.

128636.q: Why is basic insurance compulsory for everyone?
a: So that everyone is insured and the costs are shared
So that health insurers get rich
So that nobody goes to the doctor any more
So that children get more homework
128636.e: If insurance were voluntary, perhaps only sick people would join. With compulsory insurance, everyone is protected and the costs are spread.

128637.q: When does basic insurance normally pay for a medicine?
a: When it is prescribed by a doctor and on the insurer's list
Always, even sweets from the shop
Only when it is especially expensive
Only when you buy it abroad
128637.e: Basic insurance pays for medicines that a doctor prescribes and that are on an official list. You pay for many over-the-counter products yourself.
128637.m: Prescribed and listed: then the insurer pays.

128638.q: When does basic insurance pay for physiotherapy after an injury?
a: When a doctor has prescribed it
128638.e: Physiotherapy is paid for by basic insurance if it is prescribed by a doctor. The deductible and co-payment still apply.

128639.q: Leonie is on holiday in Italy and gets ill. What helps her at the doctor's there?
128639.e: The European Health Insurance Card on the back of the insurance card helps with necessary treatment in the EU and EFTA.
128639.m: In Europe: turn your card over.

128640.q: Why do families often take out travel or supplementary insurance for trips far away?
a: Because basic insurance pays only up to a limit abroad
Because you never get ill abroad
Because otherwise the plane will not take off
128640.e: Abroad, basic insurance only pays for emergencies up to a certain limit. In countries with high medical costs that can be too little.

128641.q: Which number do you dial in Switzerland for an ambulance?
128641.e: 144 is the emergency number for the ambulance service. 117 is the police, 118 the fire brigade and 1414 Rega.

128642.q: Which hospital ward does basic insurance pay for?
128642.e: Basic insurance pays for a stay on the general ward. The medical treatment there is just as good.
128642.m: General ward: good medicine for everyone.

128643.q: Which statement about recommended vaccinations for children is true?
a: Basic insurance pays for many recommended vaccinations
Only supplementary insurance pays for vaccinations
The school pays for vaccinations in full
128643.e: Basic insurance pays for many vaccinations recommended by the Confederation, for example for children. Prevention can avoid later costs.
128643.m: Prevention is part of it too.

128644.q: What can everyone do so that premiums rise less sharply?
a: Only go to the doctor when it is necessary
Buy as many medicines as possible
Go to hospital with every sniffle
128644.e: Premiums depend on health costs. Anyone who is careful about treatment and checks bills helps keep costs low.

128645.q: Where can you get neutral advice if you are in a dispute with your health insurer?
a: At the health insurance ombudsman's office
128645.e: The health insurance ombudsman's office helps free of charge and neutrally with problems between insured people and insurers.
128645.m: Dispute with your insurer? Ask the ombudsman.

128646.q: What can happen if you do not pay the premium?
a: You get reminders and debt collection may follow
You are automatically no longer insured
The insurer lets you off the premium
128646.e: Basic insurance stays compulsory, even with unpaid premiums. The insurer sends reminders and can claim the money through debt collection.

128647.q: What applies to the premium for young adults aged 19 to 25?
a: Many insurers have a lower premium
They pay no premium at all
They pay the highest premium of all
They are not allowed to be insured
128647.e: For young adults up to 25, insurers offer lower premiums than for older adults. The children's premium applies up to 18.
128647.m: Up to 25: usually a bit cheaper.

128648.q: Paul only sends his cancellation of basic insurance on 15 December. What happens?
a: He stays with the old insurer for another year
He switches at New Year anyway
He is not insured at all from January
The insurer must release him at once
128648.e: To switch on 1 January, the cancellation must arrive by the end of November. If it arrives too late, you stay with the old insurer for another year.
128648.m: Cancelling too late means waiting a year.

128649.q: What do you mainly need for the first step in the Telmed model when you have symptoms?
128649.e: Telmed stands for telemedicine. The first step is a call to the medical advice line, which then recommends what to do next.
128649.m: Telmed starts with a phone call.

128650.q: What do you often have to fill in when applying for supplementary insurance?
128650.e: For supplementary insurance, the insurer asks about your health. Then it decides whether and on what terms it will accept you.
128650.m: Supplementary: the insurer asks about your health.

128651.q: In the family doctor model, who sends you to a specialist, for example a skin doctor?
128651.e: In the family doctor model, the family doctor writes a referral when a specialist is needed. That keeps the treatment coordinated.
128651.m: The family doctor decides who helps next.

128652.q: What is the difference between the premium and the deductible?
a: You always pay the premium, the deductible only when there are costs
They are exactly the same thing
You pay the deductible every month, the premium never
Only the insurer pays the premium to you
128652.e: The premium is the fixed amount you pay regularly. You only pay the deductible when you really have treatment costs.
128652.m: Premium always, deductible only with costs.

128653.q: Marco has a deductible of 300 francs. His costs for the year are 500 francs. How much does he pay himself?
128653.e: He pays the 300 franc deductible. Of the remaining 200 francs, a 10 % co-payment is added, which is 20 francs. Together that makes 320 francs.
128653.m: First the deductible, then 10 % of the rest.

a: An accident during a football match on Sunday
128654.e: An occupational accident happens at work. The employer's accident insurance is always responsible for it.

128655.q: If the doctor's surgery bills the health insurer directly, what are you entitled to as a patient?
128655.e: Even if the surgery bills the insurer directly, it must give you a copy of the bill. That way you can check it.
128655.m: You are allowed to see every bill.

128656.q: How is a premium reduction usually paid out?
a: Directly to the health insurer, so the premium gets lower
Not at all, it is only a promise
128656.e: The canton usually pays the premium reduction directly to the health insurer. The insured people then get a lower premium bill.
128656.m: The reduction goes straight to the insurer.

128657.q: Why do young people in basic insurance help pay for the costs of older people?
a: Because everyone pays into the same pot
Because young people never have medical costs
Because older people pay no premium
Because the insurer punishes young people
128657.e: Older people often need more treatment. Because adults of all ages pay similar premiums, young people help out. Later they benefit from it themselves.
128657.m: Today I help, later I will be helped.

128658.q: Within what period must a person who moves to Switzerland take out health insurance?
a: Within three months of taking up residence
Only after the first visit to a doctor
128658.e: The KVG requires you to take out insurance within three months of taking up residence in Switzerland. The insurance then applies retroactively from the date you moved.
128658.m: New to Switzerland: three months to get health insurance.

128659.q: May a health insurer ask health questions for basic insurance?
a: No, it must accept everyone without a health check
Yes, and it may turn down people who are ill
Yes, but only for people over 50
128659.e: Basic insurance has an obligation to accept everyone. Age and state of health must play no role, which is why there are no health questions.
128659.m: Basic insurance: no health questions, no rejection.

a: An area within a canton with its own premium level
A group of insurers with the same price
128660.e: Some cantons are divided into up to three premium regions, because health costs are often higher in towns than in the countryside. So the premium can differ within one canton.
128660.m: Where you live matters: town and country can cost different amounts.

128661.q: Into which three age groups do health insurers divide premiums?
a: Children 0 to 18, young adults 19 to 25, adults from 26
Children 0 to 12, teenagers 13 to 20, adults from 21
Children 0 to 16, adults 17 to 64, seniors from 65
Children 0 to 20, adults 21 to 60, seniors from 61
128661.e: The KVG has three premium categories: children up to 18, young adults from 19 to 25 and adults from 26. Young adults usually pay less than adults.

128662.q: Noah turns 19 in January. What changes in his basic insurance?
a: He moves into the young adults' premium group
He has to take a new health check
His premium stays the same as for children
128662.e: From the year in which you turn 19, the premium for young adults applies. It is higher than the children's premium but usually lower than the premium from 26.
128662.m: At 19 the young adults' premium begins.

128663.q: Which deductible levels are there for adults in basic insurance?
128663.e: For adults, 300 francs is the standard deductible. There are also five optional deductibles up to 2500 francs, which bring a lower premium.
128663.m: From 300 to 2500: six levels for adults.

128664.q: What is the highest optional deductible for adults?
128664.e: The highest optional deductible for adults is 2500 francs. Anyone who chooses it pays the lowest premium, but pays more of the costs themselves if they fall ill.

128665.q: Which deductible levels can be chosen for children?
128665.e: For children the standard deductible is 0 francs. Parents can choose an optional deductible of 100 to 600 francs in steps of a hundred.
128665.m: Children: a deductible of 0 to 600 francs.

128666.q: Do the monthly premiums you pay count towards the deductible?
a: No, premium and deductible are separate
Yes, every premium lowers the deductible
128666.e: You pay the premium in any case. The deductible only concerns treatment costs, which you first pay yourself.
128666.m: Paying the premium does not reduce the deductible.

128667.q: Mia has a deductible of 300 and no costs so far. Her doctor's bill is 500 francs. How much does she pay herself?
128667.e: First Mia pays the deductible of 300 francs. Of the remaining 200 francs she pays a 10 % co-payment, which is 20 francs.
128667.m: First the deductible, then 10 % of the rest.

128668.q: Luca has a deductible of 2500 and a bill of 1800 francs, with no other costs in the year. What does the insurer pay?
a: Nothing, Luca pays it all himself
128668.e: The 1800 francs are below the deductible of 2500 francs. So Luca pays the whole bill himself.
128668.m: Below the deductible you pay everything yourself.

128669.q: Sara has already used up her deductible. A new bill is 400 francs. How much does she pay?
128669.e: Once the deductible has been reached, you only pay the co-payment of 10 %. For 400 francs that is 40 francs.

128670.q: An adult with a deductible of 300 has costs of 10,000 francs in a year. How much does he pay himself, not counting the hospital contribution?
128670.e: He pays 300 francs deductible. The co-payment would be 970 francs, but it is capped at 700 francs. In total that is 1000 francs.
128670.m: Deductible of 300 plus a maximum of 700 makes no more than 1000.

128671.q: What is the maximum cost-sharing per year with a deductible of 2500, not counting the hospital contribution?
128671.e: On top of the deductible of 2500 francs comes, at most, the maximum co-payment of 700 francs. Together that makes 3200 francs.
128671.m: Deductible plus 700 is the annual maximum.

128672.q: From what costs above the deductible does an adult reach the maximum co-payment?
128672.e: A 10 % co-payment on 7000 francs comes to exactly 700 francs. From then on, the insurer pays everything else, apart from the hospital contribution.

128673.q: Elias has a deductible of 1000. His costs for the year are 3000 francs. How much does he pay himself?
128673.e: Elias pays 1000 francs deductible and 10 % of the remaining 2000 francs, which is 200 francs. Together that is 1200 francs.

128674.q: What is the maximum co-payment per year for children?
128674.e: Children up to 18 also pay a 10 % co-payment, but no more than 350 francs a year, which is half the adult maximum.

128675.q: A child with a deductible of 0 has costs of 5000 francs in a year. How much do the parents pay as co-payment?
128675.e: 10 % of 5000 francs would be 500 francs. For children, however, the co-payment is capped at 350 francs a year.
128675.m: For a child it stops at 350 francs.

128676.q: Anna has a deductible of 500 and has already paid 200 francs this year. New bill: 600 francs. What does she pay for it?
128676.e: There are still 300 francs of the deductible left. Of the remaining 300 francs she pays 10 %, which is 30 francs. In total 330 francs.
128676.m: First the rest of the deductible, then 10 %.

128677.q: With a deductible of 2500, Tim saves 1400 francs in premiums per year compared with a deductible of 300. He has hardly any costs. What is true?
a: He saves money as long as he needs little treatment
He no longer receives any benefits
128677.e: Anyone who is rarely ill pays little themselves with a high deductible and saves a lot on premiums. The risk is that up to 2200 francs more deductible can be due if they fall ill.
128677.m: A high deductible pays off for healthy people with savings.

128678.q: For whom is a low deductible of 300 francs usually sensible?
a: For people with regular high treatment costs
For healthy people who never go to the doctor
For anyone who wants to save on premiums
For people with no savings and no costs
128678.e: Anyone who is chronically ill or has high costs every year will reach the deductible anyway. A low deductible then limits their own costs.
128678.m: Lots of costs: low deductible. Few costs: high deductible.

128679.q: By when must you tell the insurer that you want a lower deductible for the next year?
128679.e: A switch to a lower deductible is possible from the start of the year and must reach the insurer by 30 November. You can still choose a higher deductible until the end of December.
128679.m: Lower by 30 November, higher by 31 December.

128680.q: Can you change your deductible in the middle of the year because you suddenly fall ill?
a: No, a change is only possible from the start of the year
Yes, at any time by phone
Yes, if the doctor confirms it
128680.e: The deductible applies for the whole calendar year. Otherwise everyone would only choose the low deductible once they were ill.
128680.m: You can only change your deductible for the new year.

128681.q: How much is the hospital contribution for adults per day in hospital?
128681.e: Anyone staying in hospital as an inpatient pays 15 francs a day towards meals. The reason: at home you would also spend money on food.

128682.q: Mr Meier spends 6 days in hospital. How much hospital contribution does he pay?
128682.e: The contribution is 15 francs a day. 6 days times 15 francs makes 90 francs.

128683.q: Does the hospital contribution count towards the maximum co-payment of 700 francs?
128683.e: The hospital contribution is a separate share of the costs. It is charged in addition to the deductible and co-payment and is not included in the maximum of 700 francs.
128683.m: The hospital contribution comes on top.

128684.q: What is typical of the HMO model?
a: You are treated first at a particular health centre
You may see any specialist directly
You get dental treatment free of charge
128684.e: In the HMO model, a health centre with several specialists is the first point of contact. In return, the premium is lower than in the standard model.
128684.m: HMO: go to the health centre first.

128685.q: What do the family doctor, HMO and Telmed models have in common?
a: You give up free choice of doctor and pay lower premiums
They pay for more services than the standard model
128685.e: All alternative models have a first point of contact. The benefits stay the same, but the premium is cheaper than in the standard model.
128685.m: Less freedom of choice, lower premium.

128686.q: What does the standard model of basic insurance offer?
a: Free choice of doctor without a first point of contact
128686.e: In the standard model you may go directly to any approved doctor. This freedom has its price: the premium is usually the highest.
128686.m: Standard means free choice, but a higher premium.

128687.q: Ivo has the family doctor model and wants to see a dermatologist. What does he normally have to do?
a: Go to his family doctor first and get a referral
Go straight there without telling anyone
128687.e: In the family doctor model, the family doctor is the first point of contact. He refers you to specialists if necessary. Exceptions such as emergencies are set by the insurer.
128687.m: Family doctor model: the way to a specialist goes through your GP.

128688.q: What applies in a real emergency in the family doctor, HMO or Telmed model?
a: You may go straight to A&E without phoning first
You must reach your family doctor first
128688.e: In an emergency, the obligation to use the first point of contact does not apply. You should get help immediately, for example by calling 144.
128688.m: In an emergency, only fast help counts.

128689.q: What can happen if you repeatedly fail to follow the rules of the model you chose?
a: The insurer can cut benefits or switch you to the standard model
The insurer must lower the premium
Nothing at all, the rules are voluntary
128689.e: The lower premium is only available if you keep to the agreement. Anyone who ignores it risks cuts in benefits or exclusion from the model.
128689.m: A saving model means following the rules.

128690.q: Nina has Telmed and a sore throat. What is her first step?
a: Order a prescription on the internet
128690.e: With Telmed you phone the medical hotline before visiting a doctor. They decide whether and where you should go.

128691.q: What is decisive for cancelling on time by 30 November?
a: The cancellation must have reached the insurer by then
A postmark of 30 November is enough
A phone call on 1 December is enough
The cancellation only counts from January
128691.e: What counts is when it arrives at the health insurer, not the date it was sent. So you send the cancellation early, ideally by registered post.

128692.q: Who can also cancel basic insurance as of 30 June?
a: Anyone with a deductible of 300 and the standard model
128692.e: With the standard deductible and the standard model, you can also cancel for the end of June with three months' notice. The cancellation must then arrive by 31 March.
128692.m: A June switch only with 300 and the standard model.

128693.q: By when must the insurer announce the premiums for the next year?
a: At least two months in advance, so by the end of October
128693.e: Insurers must announce new premiums at least two months before they take effect. That leaves time until 30 November to cancel.
128693.m: New premium in October, decision by 30 November.

128694.q: When does the old basic insurance really end when you switch insurer?
a: Only when the new insurer has confirmed that it accepts you
After the first visit to a doctor
128694.e: So that nobody is left without insurance, the old insurance only ends once the new insurer has said that it insures the person.
128694.m: No gap: the old ends only when the new is confirmed.

128695.q: What applies if you still owe premiums to your insurer?
a: You can only switch once everything has been paid
You can still switch at any time
The new insurer takes over the debts
128695.e: Anyone facing debt collection who has not paid premiums or cost-sharing cannot switch insurer until the arrears have been settled.

128696.q: Jan is switching his basic insurance. Does he have to switch his supplementary insurance too?
a: No, it can stay with the current insurer
Yes, both must be with the same insurer
Yes, otherwise the basic insurance lapses
128696.e: Basic and supplementary insurance are separate contracts. You can have them with different insurers. You should not cancel the supplementary insurance too hastily, because a new health check would be needed.
128696.m: Switching basic and keeping supplementary is possible.

128697.q: Which official federal tool compares basic insurance premiums?
128697.e: The Federal Office of Public Health runs a neutral premium calculator called Priminfo. There you can see all approved premiums for your own region.

128698.q: Where is the premium reduction normally paid?
a: In cash to the insured person
128698.e: The reduction usually goes directly to the health insurer. It deducts it from the premium bill.
128698.m: The reduction lowers the premium bill.

128699.q: What does the premium reduction NOT cover?
128699.e: The premium reduction only lowers the basic insurance premium. You still have to pay your share of treatment costs yourself.
128699.m: The premium is reduced, not the deductible.

128700.q: Which statement about the premium reduction is true?
a: The rules and limits differ from canton to canton
It is the same amount throughout Switzerland
It only applies to supplementary insurance
128700.e: Each canton decides which incomes qualify and whether you have to apply. So it is worth asking your own canton.
128700.m: The premium reduction is a matter for the canton.

128701.e: Basic insurance is governed by the KVG, supplementary insurance by the VVG. So different rules apply to supplementary insurance, for example there is no obligation to accept everyone.

128702.q: What happens if you hide an illness in your application for supplementary insurance?
a: The insurer can cancel the contract and refuse benefits
128702.e: Health questions must be answered truthfully. If you breach this duty of disclosure, the insurer may withdraw from the contract.
128702.m: Always be honest with health questions.

128703.q: What is an exclusion clause (Vorbehalt) in supplementary insurance?
a: A particular illness is excluded from the benefits
An obligation to have a 2500 deductible
A free year for new customers
128703.e: If you have pre-existing conditions, the insurer can offer supplementary insurance with an exclusion. It then does not pay costs for that illness.
128703.m: An exclusion means this condition is not covered.

128704.q: What do you need semi-private or private hospital supplementary insurance for?
a: For more comfort and free choice of doctor in hospital
For the co-payment at the pharmacy
128704.e: Basic insurance pays for the general ward. Anyone who wants a two-bed or single room and a choice of hospital doctor needs supplementary insurance.
128704.m: Basic pays for the general ward, supplementary for comfort.

128705.q: Why is it worth taking out supplementary insurance while you are young?
a: You are usually healthy and are accepted without exclusions
Young people pay no basic premium
Because it is then included in basic insurance
128705.e: As you get older, the risk of pre-existing conditions grows, and insurers are more likely to refuse. Young, healthy people are usually accepted without any problem.
128705.m: Best take out supplementary insurance while you are healthy.

128706.q: Which statement about the notice periods for supplementary insurance is true?
a: They are in the contract and can differ from basic insurance
They are always the same as for basic insurance
There is never a way to cancel
You can cancel any day without notice
128706.e: For supplementary insurance, the contract terms under the VVG apply. Durations and notice periods can therefore differ from the 30 November deadline.
128706.m: Supplementary: check the notice period in the contract.

128707.q: Which law governs compulsory accident insurance for employees?
a: The UVG, the Accident Insurance Act
128707.e: All employees in Switzerland are insured under the UVG against occupational accidents and occupational diseases. The employer must register them.

128708.q: Who pays the premium for occupational accident insurance?
128708.e: The premium for occupational accidents is always paid by the employer. The premium for non-occupational accidents, however, may be deducted from the wage.

128709.q: Who usually pays the premium for non-occupational accident insurance?
a: The employees, through a deduction from their wages
128709.e: The NBU premium may be deducted from the wage. Some employers voluntarily pay all or part of it.
128709.m: You can see NBU on your payslip.

128710.q: Selin works 6 hours a week at each of two companies. Who pays for an accident in her free time?
a: Her health insurer, with deductible and co-payment
The accident insurance of the larger company
128710.e: For non-occupational accident insurance, what counts is 8 hours a week with the same employer. Selin does not reach that anywhere, so she needs accident cover through her health insurer.
128710.m: 8 hours with the same employer, not added together.

128711.q: Someone who works less than 8 hours a week has an accident on the way to work. How is the accident treated?
128711.e: For part-time work of less than 8 hours a week, accidents on the direct way to work count as occupational accidents. So the journey to work is still covered.
128711.m: Under 8 hours: the way to work counts as work.

128712.q: What can you do with your health insurer if you are insured against all accidents through your employer?
a: Exclude accident cover and save on the premium
128712.e: Anyone who works at least 8 hours a week for the same employer is also insured in their free time under the UVG. You can then suspend accident cover with your health insurer.

128713.q: Leon finishes his apprenticeship and has no job afterwards. What should he do with his health insurer?
a: Nothing, he stays insured through his training company
128713.e: Non-occupational accident cover ends 31 days after the last working day. After that, accident cover must be included again with the health insurer.
128713.m: Job gone: include accident cover with your insurer again.

a: An extension of non-occupational accident cover for up to 6 months
A contract between two health insurers
128714.e: After a job ends, you can extend UVG cover for accidents in your free time by up to 6 months with an Abredeversicherung, for example for a long journey.

128715.q: What cost-sharing is there for treatment of an accident insured under the UVG?
a: A hospital contribution of 50 francs a day
128715.e: Accident insurance under the UVG pays treatment costs without a deductible or co-payment. If the accident is only covered by the health insurer, cost-sharing does apply.

128716.q: How much daily allowance does UVG insurance pay if you are completely unable to work after an accident?
a: 100 % of the wage from the first day
128716.e: From the third day after the accident, accident insurance pays a daily allowance of 80 % of the insured earnings.

128717.q: How are self-employed people insured against accidents?
a: Not automatically under the UVG, they must make their own arrangements
128717.e: Compulsory UVG insurance applies to employees. Self-employed people have accident cover through their health insurer or can insure themselves voluntarily under the UVG.

128718.q: What does the Tiers garant system mean?
a: You pay the bill yourself and get money back from the insurer
The insurer pays the doctor directly
The bill goes to the employer
128718.e: With Tiers garant, the doctor's practice sends the bill to the patient. She pays it and submits it to the insurer, which refunds the share above the deductible and co-payment.
128718.m: Tiers garant: pay first, then claim back.

128719.q: What does the Tiers payant system mean?
a: The insurer pays directly and then asks for the cost-sharing
The patient pays everything and gets nothing back
128719.e: With Tiers payant, the provider bills the insurer directly. The insured person then receives a bill for the deductible and co-payment.
128719.m: Tiers payant: the insurer pays first.

128720.q: Where is billing usually done under Tiers payant?
a: In hospital and at the pharmacy
128720.e: Hospitals and pharmacies usually bill the health insurer directly. Doctors' practices, on the other hand, often use Tiers garant, depending on the contract.
128720.m: Pharmacy and hospital: usually directly to the insurer.

128721.q: What must you receive from the provider under Tiers payant?
a: A copy of the bill to check
128721.e: Even when the insurer pays directly, the insured person must receive a copy of the bill. That way they can check whether the services charged are correct.
128721.m: Always check the bill, even when the insurer pays.

128722.q: Lara receives a doctor's bill under Tiers garant. What does she do with it?
a: Pay it and submit it to her health insurer
Throw it away, the insurer knows about it
Only pay it if it is above the deductible
128722.e: You should also submit bills below the deductible. That is the only way the insurer knows how much of the deductible has already been used.
128722.m: Submit every bill, even small ones.

128723.q: A bill includes a treatment that never took place. What do you do?
a: Ask the practice and inform the insurer
128723.e: Insured people should check their bills. You first clear up mistakes with the practice and then report them to the health insurer.
128723.m: Wrong bill: ask, don't keep quiet.

128724.q: What does the health insurer's statement of benefits show?
a: How much the insurer pays and how much you pay yourself
The premiums of all other insurers
The tax bill for the year
128724.e: The statement of benefits lists the bill amount, deductible, co-payment and the amount the insurer covers. From this you can see what you still have to pay.
128724.m: Statement of benefits: who pays what.

128725.q: The statement says: bill 250, deductible 250, co-payment 0. What does that mean?
a: The whole bill is charged to the deductible
128725.e: If the deductible has not yet been reached, the whole amount is counted towards it. The insured person pays the 250 francs themselves.
128725.m: Below the deductible you pay everything.

128726.q: Livia's statement says: bill amount 1000 francs, of which deductible 0 francs (already used up) and co-payment 100 francs. How much does the health insurer pay?
128726.e: The deductible has already been reached, so only the 10 per cent co-payment is due, here 100 francs. The insurer covers the remaining 900 francs.
128726.m: Bill minus cost-sharing gives the insurer's share.

128727.q: The statement says “service not insured”. What does that mean?
a: The insurer does not pay this amount at all
The amount counts towards the deductible
128727.e: Services that are not insured are not in the basic insurance catalogue. They do not count towards the deductible either and must be paid in full yourself.
128727.m: Not insured means: pay it all yourself.

128728.q: Why does the insurer ask for money months after a visit to the doctor?
a: It bills the deductible and co-payment afterwards
It punishes late visits to the doctor
It is paying back the premium reduction
128728.e: With Tiers payant, the insurer first pays the whole bill. Then it asks the insured person for the cost-sharing, that is the deductible and co-payment.

128729.q: In which case does basic insurance pay for dental treatment?
a: For certain serious illnesses that could not be avoided
For a brace for cosmetic reasons
128729.e: You pay for normal dental treatment yourself or through supplementary insurance. Basic insurance only pays for certain serious illnesses; dental accidents are paid by accident insurance.
128729.m: Looking after your teeth is your own responsibility.

128730.q: Who pays when Jonas falls off his bike and loses a tooth?
128730.e: Damage to teeth from an accident is paid by accident insurance, that is UVG insurance or, for people not in work, the accident cover of the health insurer.
128730.m: A dental accident is an accident.

128731.q: Which medicines does basic insurance pay for?
a: Medicines prescribed by a doctor that are on the List of Pharmaceutical Specialities
128731.e: Basic insurance covers medicines that are prescribed by a doctor and are on the FOPH's List of Pharmaceutical Specialities. Remedies you buy yourself are paid by you.
128731.m: Prescription and the List of Specialities.

128732.q: What happens if you choose an expensive brand-name medicine even though a cheap generic exists?
a: The insurer no longer pays anything
128732.e: If there is a cheaper generic with the same active ingredient, basic insurance charges a higher co-payment for the original, unless it is medically necessary.
128732.m: Choosing a generic saves your own money.

128733.q: How much does basic insurance pay towards medically necessary patient transport?
128733.e: For medically necessary transport, basic insurance pays half the costs up to 500 francs a year. For rescues it is 50 % up to 5000 francs.
128733.m: Transport: half the costs, with an upper limit.

128734.q: Under what condition does basic insurance pay for acupuncture, for example?
a: If it is done by a doctor with additional training
128734.e: Since 2017, basic insurance has paid for five complementary medicine methods if doctors with recognised further training use them. For non-medical therapists you need supplementary insurance.
128734.m: Basic insurance: complementary medicine only from a doctor.

128735.q: Which hospital ward does basic insurance pay for?
a: The general ward of a hospital on the cantonal list
A single room with the head physician
Only hospitals in your own village
128735.e: Basic insurance pays for the general ward in hospitals on a cantonal hospital list. Hospitals in other cantons are possible, but costs are limited to the rate of your home canton.

128736.q: Which tariff structure has applied to outpatient medical services in Switzerland since 2026?
a: TARDOC together with outpatient flat rates
A free price for each practice
128736.e: On 1 January 2026, TARDOC together with outpatient flat rates replaced the old TARMED. That is why outpatient bills have looked different since 2026.

128737.q: Where do you find the European Health Insurance Card?
a: Usually on the back of your health insurance card
128737.e: Swiss health insurers print the European Health Insurance Card on the back of the insurance card. You should always carry it when travelling in Europe.
128737.m: Back of the insurance card: the European card.

128738.q: What does the European Health Insurance Card give you in an EU country?
a: Necessary treatment on the same terms as in the host country
A free flight back to Switzerland
128738.e: With the card you receive medically necessary care like the local people of the country you are visiting. It does not cover the cost of being transported home.
128738.m: In an EU country you are treated like the locals.

128739.q: How much does basic insurance pay for an emergency outside the EU and EFTA, for example in the USA?
a: At most double what the costs would be in Switzerland
128739.e: Outside the EU and EFTA, basic insurance pays for emergency treatment up to at most double the amount the treatment would have cost in Switzerland. In the USA that is often not enough.
128739.m: Long-distance trip: check your travel insurance.

128740.q: What is sensible before travelling to a country with very high hospital costs?
a: Look into travel or overseas supplementary insurance
Leave your insurance card at home
128740.e: Basic insurance only gives limited cover abroad. Supplementary travel insurance covers higher costs and often also transport home.
128740.m: Check your cover before long-distance trips.

128741.q: Ines is moving to Canada for good. What happens to her basic insurance?
a: It ends when she leaves Switzerland
It then applies worldwide without limit
128741.e: The obligation to be insured depends on living in Switzerland. Anyone who emigrates deregisters, and their basic insurance ends.
128741.m: No residence in Switzerland, no basic insurance.

128742.q: Who can you turn to free of charge if you have a dispute with your health insurer?
128742.e: The Health Insurance Ombudsman mediates neutrally and free of charge between insured people and insurers. Formally, you can also lodge an objection against a decision.
128742.m: In a dispute: the ombudsman first.

128743.q: The insurer rejects a claim with a formal decision. What can you do?
a: Lodge an objection within the deadline
Switch insurer immediately in the middle of the year
128743.e: You can lodge a written objection against a formal decision by the health insurer. The deadline is stated in the decision and is usually 30 days.

128744.q: Is daily sickness allowance insurance for loss of earnings included in basic insurance?
a: No, it is voluntary and often arranged through the employer
Yes, it pays the full wage
128744.e: Basic insurance pays for treatment, not for lost wages. Many employers take out voluntary daily sickness allowance insurance for their staff.
128744.m: Basic insurance pays for treatment, not wages.

128745.q: Which three parts make up cost-sharing in basic insurance?
128745.e: Cost-sharing is the share of treatment costs that insured people pay themselves. The premium is not part of it; it is the price of the insurance.

128746.q: What can the insurer do if someone does not pay their premiums?
a: Send reminders and start debt collection proceedings
Throw the person out of basic insurance immediately
128746.e: The insurer may not cancel basic insurance because of debts. It sends reminders and can start debt collection. Anyone who has trouble paying should look into the premium reduction early.
128746.m: Not paying leads to debt collection, not to being thrown out.

128747.q: How many members does the Federal Council, the government of Switzerland, have?
128747.e: The Federal Council is made up of seven women and men. They govern Switzerland together.

128748.q: What do you do at Eiertütschen at Easter?
a: You knock two boiled eggs against each other
You throw eggs into the air
You hide eggs in the snow
You paint eggs with your feet
128748.e: At Eiertütschen two people knock the tips of their boiled eggs together. The person whose egg stays whole wins.
128748.m: At Eiertütschen the egg that stays whole wins.

128749.q: What do many children do at Fasnacht, the Swiss carnival?
a: They dress up in a costume
128749.e: At Fasnacht young and old dress up. There are parades, loud music and lots of confetti.

128750.q: What do you carve a Räbeliechtli out of in autumn?
128750.e: A Räbe is a white turnip. You hollow it out, carve patterns into it and put a light inside. Then there is a parade.

128751.q: What is hidden in the Three Kings cake on 6 January?
128751.e: A small king figure is hidden in the Three Kings cake. Whoever finds it in their piece may wear the crown.
128751.m: Whoever finds the king is king for a day.

128752.q: What is the man made of plaited bread dough that people eat around 6 December called?
128752.e: The Grittibänz is a figure made of sweet dough, often with raisin eyes. It is eaten around Saint Nicholas Day.
128752.m: On Saint Nicholas Day there is a Grittibänz.

128753.q: What do many cows wear around their necks on the alpine pasture?
128753.e: The bell rings when the cow moves. That way the farmer can hear where his cows are in the pasture.
128753.m: The cowbell shows where the cow is.

128754.q: From what age can you take part in votes for the whole of Switzerland?
128754.e: Anyone who is Swiss and 18 years old may take part in federal votes and elections.

128755.q: What is the highest railway station in Europe, in the Bernese Alps, called?
128755.e: Jungfraujoch station is at about 3,450 metres above sea level. The Jungfrau Railway travels up through a tunnel inside the mountain.
128755.m: Europe's highest train stops at the Jungfraujoch.

128756.e: For rösti you grate potatoes and fry them in a pan until they are golden brown and crispy.
128756.m: Rösti is made from grated potatoes.

128757.q: Which town is the capital of the canton of Thurgau?
128757.e: Frauenfeld is the capital of Thurgau. The cantonal government and the Grand Council meet there. Kreuzlingen is bigger, but it is not the capital.

128758.q: Which place is the capital of the canton of Obwalden?
128758.e: Sarnen lies on Lake Sarnen and is the capital of Obwalden. Stans is the capital of the neighbouring canton of Nidwalden.
128758.m: Obwalden has Sarnen, Nidwalden has Stans.

128759.q: Which town is the capital of the canton of Basel-Landschaft?
128759.e: Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft are two cantons. The capital of Basel-Landschaft is Liestal.

128760.q: How many cantons have only half a cantonal vote in votes?
128760.e: Obwalden, Nidwalden, Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden each have half a cantonal vote. They used to be called half-cantons.
128760.m: Six cantons count only half in the majority of the cantons.

128761.q: What does the abbreviation CH stand for, for example on cars?
128761.e: CH comes from Latin: Confoederatio Helvetica means Swiss Confederation. Latin fits because it does not favour any of the four national languages.

a: Differences between German-speaking Switzerland and Romandie
An old ditch around the city of Bern
128762.e: The Röstigraben, the “rösti ditch”, is not a real ditch. It is what people call it when German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland think or vote differently.
128762.m: The Röstigraben divides opinions, not landscapes.

128763.q: Which mountain in Central Switzerland is called the “Queen of the Mountains”?
128763.e: The Rigi lies between Lake Lucerne and Lake Zug. Since 1871 a cogwheel railway has gone up it, one of the first in Europe.
128763.m: The Rigi is the Queen of the Mountains.

128764.q: In which canton do the Silvesterchläuse go from farm to farm with big bells?
128764.e: In the Appenzell Hinterland the Chläuse go round on New Year's Eve and on the old New Year's Eve, 13 January. They wear bells and sing a yodel called a Zäuerli.
128764.m: The Silvesterchläuse belong to Appenzell Ausserrhoden.

128765.q: What is the stone, weighing about 83 kilograms, that is thrown in stone putting called?
128765.e: The Unspunnen stone weighs about 83.5 kilograms. At the Unspunnen festival in Interlaken, athletes try to throw it as far as possible.
128765.m: The Unspunnen stone is the most famous stone in Switzerland.

128766.q: Which custom takes place on 1 March in villages in the Engadine?
128766.e: At Chalandamarz, children go through the village with bells and songs. They want to drive away the winter.
128766.m: At Chalandamarz the children ring in the spring.

128767.q: When is the Federal Day of Thanksgiving, Repentance and Prayer?
a: On the third Sunday in September
On the first Sunday in May
On the last Sunday in June
On the second Sunday in December
128767.e: The Federal Day of Prayer is a holiday for all denominations. It takes place every year on the third Sunday in September.
128767.m: The Federal Day of Prayer is in September.

128768.q: Into how many departments is the federal administration divided?
128768.e: Each of the seven members of the Federal Council leads a department, for example the FDFA for foreign affairs.

128769.q: What is the largest glacier in the Alps, in Valais, called?
128769.e: The Great Aletsch Glacier is about 20 kilometres long. It is part of the Jungfrau-Aletsch UNESCO World Heritage Site.
128769.m: The Aletsch is the largest glacier in the Alps.

128770.q: Where is the Federal Charter of 1291 kept today?
a: In the Museum of the Federal Charters in Schwyz
In the Federal Palace in Bern
In the National Museum in Zurich
128770.e: The original Federal Charter is in the Museum of the Federal Charters in Schwyz. It is one of the best-known documents in Swiss history.
128770.m: The Federal Charter is kept in Schwyz.

128771.q: Which three cantons are officially bilingual in German and French?
128771.e: In Bern, Fribourg and Valais, German and French are official languages. The Grisons is even trilingual.
128771.m: Bern, Fribourg and Valais officially use two languages.

128772.q: Which statement about Swiss citizenship is true?
a: You have municipal, cantonal and Swiss citizenship at the same time
It applies only to the canton where you live
It is renewed every ten years
128772.e: Citizenship has three levels. Anyone who is Swiss has a place of origin, which means they are a citizen of a municipality and a canton.

128773.q: Which Swiss custom was the first to be added to the UNESCO list of intangible cultural heritage, in 2017?
128773.e: The Basel Carnival, with the Morgestraich, its cliques and satirical verses, was added to the UNESCO list in 2017 as the first Swiss element.
128773.m: The Basel Carnival is UNESCO cultural heritage.

128774.q: What must you not throw into the toilet?
128774.e: Wet wipes do not dissolve in water. They block the pipes. They belong in the bin.
128774.m: Only toilet paper goes into the toilet.

128775.q: Where do you take empty batteries?
a: To the battery collection in the shop
128775.e: Batteries contain substances that harm nature. Many shops have a collection box for them.
128775.m: Empty batteries belong in the collection box.

128776.q: The yoghurt is one day past its “best before” date. What do you do?
a: Look at it, smell it and taste it carefully
Throw it away unopened at once
128776.e: “Best before” means it is definitely fine until then. It is often still good to eat afterwards. Check it with your eyes, nose and tongue.
128776.m: Look, smell and taste instead of throwing away.

128777.q: How do you carry a knife safely through the kitchen?
128777.e: If the point faces down, you cannot hurt anyone by accident. Walk slowly while you do it.
128777.m: Always keep the knife point facing down.

128778.q: Which of these is a vegetable?
128778.e: Broccoli is a green vegetable. Apple, cherry and pear are fruits.
128778.m: Broccoli is a vegetable, the apple is a fruit.

128779.q: Your old toy is still good, but you would like something new. What is kind to the environment?
128779.e: When you swap, you have something new to play with, and nothing is thrown away. This way fewer new things are needed.
128779.m: Swapping is better than throwing away.

128780.q: What do you do when you leave a room and nobody else is in it?
128780.e: A light in an empty room uses electricity for nothing. With one click of the switch, you help save energy.
128780.m: When you go out, switch the light off.

128781.q: What do you use to wash dishes clean by hand?
128781.e: Warm water and washing-up liquid loosen grease and food leftovers. Then you rinse the dishes and let them dry.
128781.m: Warm water and washing-up liquid get things clean.

128782.q: Where do your dirty socks belong?
128782.e: In the laundry basket you collect dirty clothes until they are washed. This keeps your room tidy.
128782.m: Dirty laundry goes in the laundry basket.

128783.q: Which animal does the milk you usually buy in the shop come from?
128783.e: Most milk in Switzerland comes from cows. Butter, cheese and yoghurt are also made from milk.
128783.m: Milk usually comes from the cow.

a: Cares for sick people in hospital
128784.e: Polymechanics drill, mill and turn metal parts. They often work with computer-controlled machines.
128784.m: Polymechanics make parts out of metal.

128785.q: What does a healthcare assistant do?
a: Cares for and looks after people in hospital or a care home
128785.e: A healthcare assistant helps sick and elderly people, for example by measuring temperature and blood pressure, and helps with washing and eating.
128785.m: The healthcare assistant looks after people.

a: Furniture and windows out of wood
128786.e: Joiners saw, plane and glue wood. This is how tables, cupboards, doors and windows are made.

128787.q: What does an electrician do in a new house?
a: Lays electric cables and fits sockets
128787.e: Electricians make sure the lights work in a house and that electricity comes out of the sockets. They work very carefully because electricity is dangerous.
128787.m: The electrician brings electricity into the house.

128788.q: Where does a social care worker often work?
a: In a nursery with small children
128788.e: A social care worker plays, does crafts and eats with children at the nursery. Some also look after elderly people or people with disabilities.
128788.m: Social care workers work in nurseries.

a: Plants and looks after flowers, trees and lawns
128789.e: Gardeners work outside with plants. They lay out gardens, cut hedges and mow lawns.

128790.q: What does a retail specialist do in a shop?
a: Advises customers and fills the shelves
128790.e: Retail specialists advise customers, work at the till and make sure the goods are neat and tidy on the shelves.
128790.m: In a shop, retail specialists help you.

128791.q: Where does a cook usually work?
a: In an office full of files
128791.e: Cooks prepare vegetables, fry meat and arrange the food nicely on plates. They work in restaurants, hospitals or canteens.
128791.m: The cook cooks in a restaurant.

128792.q: Who usually pays for the school building you go to?
128792.e: In Switzerland, state schools are paid for with tax money. The municipality usually looks after the school building.
128792.m: My school was built with taxes.

128793.q: Where does your teacher's salary come from?
a: From the children in the class
128793.e: Teachers at state schools are paid with tax money. That way school costs families nothing.

128794.q: Why don't parents have to pay school fees for state school?
a: Because it is paid for with taxes
Because the school is a company
128794.e: State school is free for all children. This is possible because everyone pays taxes together.

128795.q: Mia is playing at the playground in the park. Who usually paid for the slide?
128795.e: Public playgrounds are usually built and looked after by the municipality. The money for this comes from taxes.

128796.q: What are most roads built and repaired with?
128796.e: Roads belong to everyone. The municipality, canton and Confederation pay for them with taxes and other charges.

128797.q: Who pays the police officers' salaries?
a: The people who call for help
128797.e: The police help everyone. That is why they are paid with tax money and not by the people who happen to need help.
128797.m: The police help everyone, and everyone pays.

128798.q: A child calls 117 because they need help. Do they have to pay the police anything afterwards?
a: No, the help is paid for with taxes
Only if it is a Sunday
128798.e: The police are paid with tax money. Anyone in trouble may call 117 and will get help.

128799.q: Which emergency number is for the fire brigade?
128799.e: You can reach the fire brigade on 118. It is organised by the municipality and paid for partly with taxes.
128799.m: If there is a fire, call 118.

128801.q: Lukas borrows a book from the local library. Who helps to pay for the library?
128801.e: Many libraries are supported by the municipality with tax money. That is why borrowing is often free or very cheap for children.
128801.m: Taxes fill the library with books.

128802.q: Why does it often cost only a little to get into the local swimming pool?
a: Because the municipality pays part with taxes
Because the lifeguard works for free
Because the children do the cleaning
128802.e: A swimming pool costs a lot of money. The municipality pays part of it with taxes, so entry is cheap.

128803.q: Who makes sure that the rubbish is collected regularly?
128803.e: The municipality organises rubbish collection. It is paid for with charges, for example for rubbish bags, and partly with taxes.

128804.q: In many municipalities you buy special rubbish bags. Why are they more expensive than normal bags?
a: The price includes a charge for collection
128804.e: With the price of these charged bags you pay part of the rubbish collection. People who make less rubbish pay less.

128805.q: Who helps to pay for public hospitals?
128805.e: Hospitals are paid for by health insurance and by the canton. The canton uses tax money for this.
128805.m: The canton helps pay for hospitals.

128806.q: In the town park, flowers are planted and benches repaired. Who usually pays for that?
128806.e: Parks belong to everyone. That is why the municipality pays for their upkeep with tax money.
128806.m: The park is there for everyone.

128807.q: A new bridge is being built over the river. Where does the money come from?
a: From the state, so from taxes
128807.e: Large structures like bridges are paid for by the municipality, canton or Confederation. The money comes from taxes.
128807.m: Bridges connect, and taxes pay for them.

128808.q: Who pays for buses and trains?
a: Passengers with tickets and the state with taxes
128808.e: Tickets don't cover all the costs. The rest is paid by the municipality, canton and Confederation with tax money.
128808.m: Tickets plus taxes: that's how the bus runs.

128809.q: Why is a bus ticket cheaper than what the journey really costs?
a: Because tax money pays part of it
Because the bus doesn't need fuel
128809.e: Buses and trains cost a lot. The state pays part with taxes so that everyone can travel cheaply.

128810.q: Who pays taxes on their wages?
128810.e: Anyone who works and gets a wage pays part of it as taxes. People who earn more pay more.
128810.m: If you earn a wage, you pay taxes.

a: Yes, companies pay taxes on their profits
128811.e: Not only people but companies pay taxes too. They pay on the money they have earned.

a: The village or town where you live
128812.e: The municipality is your village or your town. It looks after things near you, such as school and playgrounds.
128812.m: The municipality is very close to me.

128813.q: What do people mean when they talk about the “Confederation”?
128813.e: The “Confederation” means the state of the whole of Switzerland. It looks after things that are important for the whole country.
128813.m: The Confederation is the whole of Switzerland.

128814.q: In which city does the Swiss government work?
128814.e: The Swiss government, the Federal Council, works in Bern. Bern is the federal city.
128814.m: The Confederation is based in Bern.

128815.e: The municipality is in the canton, and all the cantons together make up the Confederation, that is Switzerland.
128815.m: Municipality, canton, Confederation: small, medium, large.

128816.e: The municipality is the smallest level. Several municipalities together make up a canton.
128816.m: The municipality is the smallest level.

128817.q: Who usually looks after the playground in your neighbourhood?
128817.e: The municipality looks after things that are close by. These include playgrounds and neighbourhood streets.
128817.m: What's close by is done by the municipality.

128818.q: Who pays for the motorways in Switzerland?
128818.e: Motorways are important for the whole country. That is why the Confederation looks after them.

128819.q: Who is responsible for the Swiss army?
128819.e: The army protects the whole country. That is why the Confederation pays for it with tax money.
128819.m: The army belongs to the Confederation.

128820.q: In Switzerland, who do the police usually belong to?
128820.e: Almost every canton has its own cantonal police. The canton pays for it with tax money.
128820.m: The police are usually paid for by the canton.

128822.q: What is the tax called that is included in the price of many things in a shop?
128822.e: VAT is already included in the price of many goods. The shop passes it on to the Confederation.
128822.m: VAT is included in the price.

128823.q: Where can you see how much VAT you have paid?
128823.e: The receipt often shows in small print how much VAT is included in the price. In Switzerland it is abbreviated MWST.

128824.q: Who does the shop pass the VAT money on to?
128824.e: The shop collects VAT when it sells things. Then it passes it on to the Confederation.
128824.m: The shop collects, the Confederation receives.

128826.q: Why do lots of people pay taxes together?
a: So that together they can pay for expensive things for everyone
So that nobody has to work any more
128826.e: One family alone can't pay for a school or a bridge. Together everyone can manage it.

128827.q: Could one family alone pay for a whole hospital?
a: No, that needs money from many people
128827.e: A hospital costs a great deal of money. Only if many people pay together is there enough.
128827.m: Many small contributions add up to a lot.

128828.q: In Switzerland, people who earn a lot pay ...
a: more taxes than someone with a low wage
taxes only once in their life
128828.e: People who earn more money can contribute more. That is why they pay more taxes. This is a fair way of sharing.
128828.m: Those who have more give more.

128829.q: Which statement about taxes is true?
a: Everyone helps so that everyone is well off
Only one person pays for everything
Taxes are only for the king
128829.e: With taxes everyone shares the costs of schools, roads and help. That way the whole community is better off.

128830.q: The class collects money for a trip: each child gives something. What is this like?
128830.e: With taxes, each person also gives a share, and something for everyone is paid for with it. Just like the class kitty.
128830.m: Taxes are like a big class kitty.

128831.q: Adults work and get a wage. What do they do with part of it?
a: They give it to the school
They have to give it to the bank
They pay the police directly with it
128831.e: Part of a wage goes as taxes to the municipality, canton and Confederation. Things for everyone are paid for with it.
128831.m: Part of your wage becomes tax.

128832.q: What is the office that collects taxes called?
128832.e: The tax office works out how much someone has to pay and collects the money.
128832.m: The tax office collects the taxes.

128833.q: Your parents are sitting at the table filling in papers about their wages. What are they probably doing?
128833.e: In the tax return, adults write down how much they have earned. Then it is worked out how much tax they pay.
128833.m: The tax return shows what you have earned.

128834.q: How often do adults in Switzerland normally fill in their tax return?
128834.e: The tax return is done once a year. You write down what you earned the previous year.

128835.q: Does a child with pocket money have to fill in a tax return?
128835.e: Children don't do their own tax return. Adults do that. But when shopping, children pay VAT too.

128836.q: Who usually makes sure that clean water comes out of the tap?
128836.e: The municipality looks after the water pipes. This is mainly paid for with charges for the water.
128836.m: Clean water thanks to the municipality.

128837.q: Who pays for the street lights that shine at night?
a: The people who go for walks at night
128837.e: Street lights make the way safe at night. They are usually paid for by the municipality with tax money.

128838.q: A zebra crossing in front of the school is being repainted. Who pays for this?
128838.e: Zebra crossings are part of the road. The municipality or canton pays for them with taxes.
128838.m: Safe routes to school cost money.

128839.q: In winter a snowplough clears the road. Who pays for the snowplough?
a: The municipality or canton, with taxes
128839.e: So that roads are safe in winter, the municipality and canton clear the snow. They pay for this with taxes.

128840.q: At state school, who often pays for the school books?
128840.e: At state school, children get many school books without having to buy them. This is paid for with tax money.
128840.m: School books are often paid for by taxes.

128841.q: The school gym is getting new mats. Where does the money usually come from?
a: From the children in the class
128841.e: The gym belongs to the school. The municipality pays for new equipment with taxes.

128842.q: Which number do you call if someone is badly injured?
128842.e: On 144 you reach the ambulance service. Emergency numbers are important for everyone.

128843.e: You can reach the police on 117. The police are paid for with tax money.

128844.q: What is the number of Rega, which helps by helicopter?
128844.e: Rega rescues people by helicopter. You can reach it on 1414.

128845.q: What do you get back for your taxes?
a: Things everyone uses, like schools and roads
128845.e: You don't get a present of your own for taxes. Instead there are schools, roads, police and much more for everyone.

128846.q: There is a public toilet in the park. Who usually pays for it?
128846.e: Many public toilets are built and cleaned by the municipality. The money often comes from taxes.

128847.q: Who helps to make sure that hiking trails are marked in yellow and kept in good condition?
128847.e: Hiking trails are looked after by cantons, municipalities and hiking associations. Part of the money comes from taxes.

128848.q: There are rubbish bins in the park. Who empties them?
128848.e: The municipality puts up rubbish bins and has them emptied. This is paid for partly with taxes.
128848.m: Rubbish in the bin, and the municipality collects it.

128849.q: What happens if lots of people throw rubbish on the ground?
a: The municipality has to pay more for clearing up
128849.e: Clearing up costs money, and that often comes from taxes. Anyone who disposes of rubbish properly helps everyone.
128849.m: Rubbish in the bin saves money for everyone.

128850.q: Why shouldn't you break anything in the park?
a: Everyone pays for the repair with their taxes
Because only adults are allowed there
Because the park belongs to the Confederation
128850.e: Benches and play equipment in the park are paid for with taxes. If they get broken, everyone pays for the repair.
128850.m: We protect what belongs to everyone.

128851.q: Who often provides the collection point for glass and aluminium?
128851.e: Many municipalities have collection points for glass, aluminium and paper. That way things can be recycled.
128851.m: Glass and aluminium go to the collection point.

128852.q: Ben says: “I never go to the swimming pool, so I don't need taxes.” What is true?
a: He still uses roads, school and more
He is right, he doesn't need anything
Taxes are only for swimming pools
He only has to pay dog tax
128852.e: Taxes pay for lots of different things. Even people who don't go swimming use schools, roads and hospitals.
128852.m: Everyone uses something that taxes pay for.

128853.q: Why is it fair that people with low wages pay less tax?
a: They need their money for food and housing
128853.e: People who earn little need most of their money for the essentials. That is why they pay less tax.
128853.m: Everyone gives as much as they can.
